1.open: Think of a time you waited a long time for something. What was it, and how did the waiting feel?
questions: Luke says he "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" so Theophilus could "know the certainty" of what he had been taught (vv. 3, 4). Why might certainty matter to someone who is just starting out in faith?
Zechariah and Elizabeth were "righteous in the sight of God," yet they had no children (vv. 6, 7). How does that sit with you, that faithful people still face long disappointments?

Zechariah asked, "How can I be sure of this?" (v. 18), and was left unable to speak. Mary asked, "How can this be," and the angel answered her kindly (v. 34). What differences do you notice between the two questions, and what do you make of how each was handled?

Gabriel tells Mary, "you have found favor with God" (v. 30), and she was "greatly troubled" at first (v. 29). When has good news from God, or a call to something big, felt unsettling before it felt joyful?

Mary calls herself the Lord's servant and asks that it happen to her "according to your word" (v. 38). What do you think it cost her to say that, and what would it look like for us to say something like it?
Verse 37 says, "no word from God will ever fail." Where is that easy for you to believe, and where is it harder? Be as honest as you like, including if it feels distant right now.
In her song Mary says God "has exalted the humble" and "filled the hungry with good things" (vv. 52, 53). Who do you think she was thinking of, and who might hear those words as good news today?
When Zechariah finally speaks, the first thing he does is praise God (v. 64). After a long silence, what might it do to a person to start with thanks?
1.life: Pick one thing you are waiting on or finding hard to believe. Each day this week, tell God about it in one honest sentence, the way Zechariah and Mary both brought their questions, then listen for a few quiet minutes.
1.prayer: Thank God that he keeps his promises and welcomes honest questions. Ask for trust to say to him, "May it happen to me according to your word", and pray for anyone in the group who is waiting right now.
1.tip: Questions 3 and 6 can make doubters feel judged if the group decides Zechariah was simply bad and Mary was simply good. Point out that both asked honest questions, that Luke does not explain every difference, and that the chapter ends with Zechariah praising God. Also, Christians differ on how much honor Mary should receive, with Catholic and Orthodox traditions giving her a special ongoing role and many Protestants seeing her mainly as a model of faith. Say that in one line, then keep the focus on what she says about God.

2.open: What is a family tradition at this time of year, or any time, that you would hate to give up?
questions: Luke begins with an emperor and a census, then moves to a couple with a newborn who "laid Him in a manger" (v. 7). Why do you think God chose such a humble start for the Savior?

The angel's news came to shepherds working the night shift, and the angel said it was "good news of great joy that will be for all the people" (v. 10). What does it say about God that he told them first?

The only sign the shepherds get is "a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger" (v. 12). What do you make of a sign that ordinary? When have you been asked to trust something that did not look impressive?

After they saw the child, the shepherds "spread the message" (v. 17), while Mary "treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart" (v. 19). Which of those two is more like you right now, and why?

Mary and Joseph offered "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" (v. 24), the offering for families who could not afford more. What does it mean to you that Jesus was born into an ordinary, not wealthy, family?

Simeon says the child will be "a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel" (v. 32), and also warns that "a sword will pierce your soul as well" (v. 35). Why might Luke include a hard word in the middle of a joyful story?

Simeon and Anna waited many years, and Anna "worshiped night and day" (v. 37). If you are in a season of waiting, or of doubt about whether God is doing anything, what is that like for you? You can answer honestly, even if the answer is mixed.

At twelve, Jesus asks, "Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?" and his parents "did not understand" (vv. 49, 50). Where do you find it hard to understand what God is doing, and what helps you keep going anyway?
2.life: Pick one small, ordinary moment this week and set aside five quiet minutes to ponder it, as Mary did, asking where God might be in it. Write down one thing you notice, and share it with someone if you feel like it.
2.prayer: Thank God for coming to us in a humble, ordinary way. Ask for patience in any season of waiting and for the willingness to tell someone good news this week.
2.tip: This chapter is long and familiar, so people may stay on the Christmas card version. Pick two or three sections instead of covering everything, and point to the quieter details, like the poor family's offering, the waiting of Simeon and Anna, and the parents' confusion at the end. Mention that scholars still discuss how the census fits Roman records, then move on so it does not take over the evening.

3.open: Think of someone who once told you something you needed to hear, even though it was hard. What made you listen?
questions: Luke begins by naming emperors, governors and high priests, then says "the word of God came to John" in the wilderness (v. 2). Why might Luke start with real names and dates? What does it say about where God chooses to speak?

John tells the crowds, "Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance" (v. 8). What is the difference between feeling sorry and actually changing? Where have you seen the difference in your own life?

Some people were leaning on the thought, "We have Abraham as our father" (v. 8). What do people lean on today instead of a real change of heart, like family background, church attendance or being a decent person?
When the crowds ask, "What then should we do?" John starts with sharing clothes and food (vv. 10-11). What stands out to you about how ordinary his answers are?

John told tax collectors and soldiers to stop taking more than was fair (vv. 13-14). What kinds of unfairness come easiest to someone in your job or stage of life? What might the "fair" version look like?
John says he is not worthy to untie the sandals of the One who is coming (v. 16). Why do you think John was so ready to point away from himself? What makes that hard to do?

At Jesus' baptism the voice says, "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased" (v. 22). This comes before Jesus has done any public work. What do you make of that, and how does it sit with you when you think about how God sees you?
John's honest words to Herod ended with him in prison (vv. 19-20). If you are unsure what to make of that, or of a God who lets it happen, what questions would you want to ask?
3.life: John's advice was specific and practical. This week, pick one small, concrete thing to do: share something you have extra of, or stop one small habit of taking more than your share, whether time, credit or money.
3.prayer: Ask God to show you one area where your life needs to change, and to give you the grace to take a real step. Thank him for the words spoken over Jesus, and ask to hear his love for you more clearly.
3.tip: Verses 7 to 9 and 17 sound harsh, and some people will react to the talk of fire and an axe. Don't rush past it or soften it. Name that John is blunt, then steer the group back to verses 10 to 14, where his answers are simple and doable, and to verse 18, where Luke calls all of this "good news."

4.open: Who is someone from your past who still sees you the way you were years ago, and how does that feel?
questions: Luke says Jesus was "full of the Holy Spirit" and then "led by the Spirit into the wilderness" (vv. 1-2). Why do you think the Spirit led him into a hard place, and what does that say about times when life feels like a wilderness?
The devil's first test comes when Jesus is hungry (vv. 2-3). Where are we most open to temptation: when we are tired, hungry, lonely or stressed? What have you noticed about yourself?

Each time, Jesus answers with a line from Scripture, such as "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (v. 8). The devil also quotes Scripture in verses 10 and 11. What does that tell us about how to use the Bible well?

In Nazareth Jesus reads that God "has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor" and "to release the oppressed" (v. 18). What would that sound like to someone who is poor, trapped or worn out today?
Christians differ on whether this promise is mainly about forgiveness and inner freedom, or also about real economic and social change. Where do you lean, and what might the other view help you see?
At first the crowd "marveled at the gracious words" (v. 22), but soon they were "enraged" (v. 28). What changed, and when have you wanted Jesus on your own terms?
Jesus tells his neighbors that God sent help to a foreign widow and a Syrian commander (vv. 25-27). Why might that have stung, and who do we find it hard to believe God cares about?

In verse 42 Jesus goes to "a solitary place" and then says, "I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well" (v. 43). What is one honest thing you find hard about faith, rest or purpose right now, and what would help?
4.life: Jesus kept to his custom of worship and went off alone to pray. This week, choose one small, regular habit like a quiet ten minutes, and ask God to meet you there. If faith feels hard, simply tell God so.
4.prayer: Thank God for Jesus, who faced testing and stayed faithful. Ask for help in the places where you feel tempted, and for open hearts toward people we tend to overlook.
4.tip: Question 5 can turn into a political debate. Say up front that faithful Christians disagree, let two or three people share briefly, then return to the text and ask what Jesus' words mean for how we treat people this week.

5.open: Who is someone who showed up for you when you really needed help, and what did they do?
questions: Simon says, "we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets" (v. 5). When have you done something out of trust in Jesus even though it did not make sense to you?

When the nets fill, Peter says, "Go away from me, Lord," and calls himself "a sinful man" (v. 8). Why do you think a miracle made him feel this way, and when have you felt out of your depth in front of something bigger than you?
Jesus answers Peter with "Do not be afraid" and then gives him a new job (v. 10). What does that response tell you about how Jesus treats people who feel unworthy?

A man covered with leprosy says, "Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean," and Jesus "reached out His hand and touched the man" (vv. 12, 13). Why would that touch have mattered so much to him, and who today might be going without that kind of welcome?
Verse 16 says Jesus "frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray," right after crowds began pressing in. What does that make you think about your own pace of life and where you find quiet?
The friends of the paralyzed man cut through a roof to reach Jesus, and Jesus "saw their faith" (v. 20). Who has carried you to Jesus in some way, or who might you carry this week?

The Pharisees and the scribes complained that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, and Jesus replied, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick" (v. 31). Where do you find it easy to see yourself as the patient, and where do you find it harder?
Jesus says new wine must go into new wineskins (v. 38). Christians read these sayings in different ways, so what do you think he means, and is there anything you find hard to let him change?
5.life: Think of one person who feels left out or looked down on, at work, school, church or your street. This week, share a meal or a coffee with them, and simply listen.
5.prayer: Thank Jesus that he draws near to people who feel unworthy and unclean. Ask him for honesty about where you need healing, and for the courage to welcome others the way he welcomes you.
5.tip: Questions 2 and 7 can stir up shame or defensiveness. Let people answer lightly or pass, and remind the group that in this chapter Jesus meets every honest admission with welcome, never with rejection. Do not try to settle the wineskin saying in verse 38 or the last line in verse 39; Christians read them in different ways, so hold them loosely.

6.open: Who is someone who treated you with unexpected kindness, and what did they do?
questions: The Pharisees ask, "Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?" (v. 2). Jesus answers with a story about David and then says, "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (v. 5). What do you think Jesus is saying about the purpose of rules and rest?

Before the man with the withered hand is healed, Jesus asks, "which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?" (v. 9). When have you seen rules, habits or traditions get in the way of simply helping someone?

Jesus says, "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (v. 20), and then, "woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort" (v. 24). What do you find encouraging or uncomfortable about hearing both?
Jesus says, "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you" (v. 27). Who comes to mind when you hear that? Be as honest as you like, including if you are not sure you want to do it.
In verse 35 Jesus says God "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked." How does it change the way you see God, or other people, that his kindness reaches that far?

Verses 29 and 30 talk about turning the other cheek and giving to everyone who asks. Christians read these differently, some as strict commands and some as a posture of the heart. How do you hear them, and where do you think kindness ends and being used begins?
Jesus asks, "Why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?" (v. 41). Why is it so much easier to see other people's faults than our own?

Jesus asks, "Why do you call Me 'Lord, Lord,' but do not do what I say?" (v. 46). Where is there a gap between what you hear or believe and what you actually do? You can answer with a doubt or a struggle if that is more honest.
6.life: Pick one person who is hard for you to love, and this week do one small, quiet good thing for them or pray for them by name each day. Verse 36 is the goal: "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful."
6.prayer: Thank God that he is kind even to the ungrateful, and that includes us. Ask him for mercy toward the person who is hardest to love, and for the strength to act on what we have heard.
6.tip: Verses 29 and 30 can lead to a debate or to guilt, especially for anyone who has been hurt or taken advantage of. Say early that Christians read these verses differently, and make clear that mercy is not the same as staying in an unsafe situation. Then bring the group back to verse 36 and the heart behind the commands.

7.open: Think of a time someone welcomed you warmly when you didn't expect it. What did they do?
questions: The centurion says, "I am not worthy to have You come under my roof" (v. 6), and yet the Jewish elders say he is worthy (v. 4). Why might he and others see him so differently?

He says, "just say the word, and my servant will be healed" (v. 7). Jesus says, "not even in Israel have I found such great faith" (v. 9). What do you think made this trust so striking, coming from an outsider?
At Nain, Jesus sees a grieving widow and says, "Do not weep" (v. 13). What does this scene show you about how Jesus responds to people in pain?

John sends this question: "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" (v. 19). Scholars differ on whether John was doubting himself. Either way, when have you had questions about Jesus, and how did you handle them?

Jesus answers John by pointing to what he is doing, including that "the good news is preached to the poor" (v. 22), and adds, "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me" (v. 23). What do you hear in that answer? What might make someone stumble over Jesus?
Simon thinks, "If this man were a prophet" he would never let such a woman touch him (v. 39). Where do you see people sorted into who deserves attention and who doesn't, in the church or outside it?

Jesus says, "her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much" (v. 47). Christians read that line in two ways: some see her love as the result of forgiveness already received, and others see her love and faith as part of what brought it. How does the story of the two debtors help you think about it?
The guests ask, "Who is this who even forgives sins?" (v. 49), and Jesus tells her, "Your faith has saved you; go in peace" (v. 50). What would going in peace look like for you right now?
7.life: This week, pay attention to one person who tends to be overlooked, such as a coworker, a neighbor or someone at church. Greet them by name and give them real time and attention, the kind of welcome Simon failed to give.
7.prayer: Thank Jesus that no one is too far outside for him to notice. Ask him to show you where you have trusted him like the centurion, where you are still asking questions like John, and where you need his forgiveness and peace.
7.tip: Questions 4 and 7 can pull the group in different directions. Let honest doubt be welcome without rushing to fix it, and on verse 47 say plainly that Christians read it two ways, then bring the group back to the two debtors and what Jesus does for the woman.

8.open: When you were a kid, what is something you were afraid of at night, and what helped you feel better?
questions: Verses 2 and 3 name women who had been healed and who supported Jesus "out of their own means." What does it tell you that Jesus' work was carried by ordinary people giving what they had?
Jesus says, "The seed is the word of God" (v. 11). Of the four soils, which one sounds most like you in this season of life, and what makes you say so?
The seed on rocky ground is received "with joy," but has "no root" (v. 13). What helps a person's faith grow roots, and what helps in your own life?

Verse 10 is hard to read, and Christians understand it differently: some think God deliberately hides understanding from some people, others think the parables simply show a closed attitude that was already there. How does that verse land with you?
Jesus says, "Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen" (v. 18). What is one practical thing that changes how well you listen to God or to Scripture?
In the storm Jesus asks, "Where is your faith?" (v. 25). Is that a rebuke, a gentle question, or something else to you? Tell about a time you felt like the boat was going under and God seemed asleep.

The healed man in verse 39 is told to "describe how much God has done for you," while the townspeople ask Jesus to leave because of fear (v. 37). Why might a good thing still frighten people, and what do you do when change feels scary?

Jesus stops for a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years and calls her "Daughter" (v. 48), even while Jairus is waiting. What does that moment show you about how Jesus sees people, and what do you make of it if you are not sure he sees you that way?
8.life: Pick one thing that tends to crowd out your time with God, such as worry, work or your phone. This week, set aside ten quiet minutes a day to read a short passage and ask God what to take from it.
8.prayer: Ask God to make your heart good soil, ready to hear and hold on to his word. Pray for anyone in the group who feels caught in a storm tonight.
8.tip: The storm and the healing stories can leave people with hard questions about prayers that did not end well. Do not rush to explain. Let honest doubt be spoken, point to the disciples' own frightened question, "Who is this?" (v. 25), and keep the focus on who Jesus is rather than on formulas.

9.open: Think of a trip you took. What is one thing you forgot to bring, and how did it turn out?
questions: Jesus tells the Twelve, "Take nothing for the journey" (v. 3). They had to depend on the kindness of strangers. What might that have taught them, and where do you find it hard to depend on anyone?

When the crowd is hungry, Jesus says, "You give them something to eat" (v. 13). All the disciples have is five loaves and two fish. What do you have that feels too small to matter, and what would it look like to offer it anyway?
Jesus asks, "Who do you say I am?" (v. 20). If a friend asked you that today, how would you honestly answer? It is fine to say you are not sure.
Peter names Jesus as "The Christ of God" (v. 20), and Jesus straight away says he must suffer and be killed (v. 22). Why might that have been hard for Peter to hear?

Jesus says, "he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me" (v. 23). Christians differ on whether his hardest demands in this chapter apply literally to every follower or describe a special calling and an attitude of putting him first. What do you hear him asking of you?
On the mountain a voice says, "This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!" (v. 35). What gets in the way of really listening to Jesus in your daily life?

Right after the mountain, the disciples argue about "which of them would be the greatest" (v. 46). Jesus answers with a child (v. 48). Where do you catch yourself comparing or ranking, and what might change if you took Jesus' answer seriously?

John wants to stop an outsider, and Jesus says, "whoever is not against you is for you" (v. 50). James and John want to call down fire on a village, and Jesus rebukes them (v. 55). How should we treat people who reject us or do things differently from us?
9.life: Pick one small thing you have, such as an hour, a meal or a phone call, and give it to someone this week. Trust Jesus with what happens next. Each morning, say Jesus' question from verse 20 aloud and give God one honest sentence in reply.
9.prayer: Ask God for honesty in answering who Jesus is to you, even where you have doubts. Ask for ears to listen to him and willingness to follow.
9.tip: This chapter is long and full of hard sayings, so do not try to cover it all. Spend most of your time on verses 18 to 26. If verses 59 and 60 come up, say that scholars are unsure whether the man's father had already died, and that Jesus is not mocking grief. Keep the focus on what following him asks of us.

10.open: Think of a time a stranger helped you when you did not expect it. What did they do?
questions: Jesus says, "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few" (v. 2). What do you think he means by the harvest, and what might it look like for ordinary people like us to be workers in it?
He sends them out "like lambs among wolves" (v. 3) and tells them to carry no purse or bag. Why might Jesus ask them to go with so little, and what would be hardest for you about that?

The seventy-two come back full of joy about their success, but Jesus says to "rejoice that your names are written in heaven" (v. 20). Why might he steer them away from celebrating their power? Where do you tend to find your sense of worth?
The expert in the law answers well: love God fully and "Love your neighbor as yourself" (v. 27). Which of those two feels harder to you right now, and why?
The man asks, "And who is my neighbor?" (v. 29), and Jesus answers with a story. Why do you think Jesus tells a story instead of giving a simple definition?

The priest and the Levite "passed by on the other side" (vv. 31-32). The text does not say why. What reasons might people give today for walking past someone in need, and which one sounds most like you?

The Samaritan "had compassion" and then paid real cost with his time, his animal and his money (vv. 33-35). Who would be the last person you would want help from? How would it feel if they were the one who stopped for you?

Martha says, "Lord, do You not care?" (v. 40) and Jesus says Mary "has chosen the good portion" (v. 42). Where do you feel pulled between busyness and sitting still with God? If you are not sure what sitting with God even looks like, or it feels distant, what is that like for you?
10.life: This week, notice one person you would normally pass by, a neighbor, a coworker or someone who is hard to like. Do one small, practical thing for them. Then set aside ten quiet minutes to simply sit and listen for God, like Mary.
10.prayer: Ask God to open your eyes to the person in your path who needs mercy. Ask for a heart that can slow down and listen to Jesus, and thank him that our names are written in heaven.
10.tip: The Good Samaritan is so familiar that people may skip straight to a quick moral. Slow down on verse 29 and the Samaritan's identity, and let people name who feels like an unlikely neighbor today. Also note that Christians read the story differently: some see mainly an example of how to treat others, while others also see a picture of Jesus rescuing wounded humanity. You do not need to settle that tonight. Be gentle with the Martha question, since busy people can hear it as criticism.

11.open: What is something you have borrowed from a neighbor or friend, and how did they respond?
questions: A disciple asks, "Lord, teach us to pray" (v. 1). If you could ask Jesus to teach you one thing about prayer, what would it be?

The prayer opens with "Father, hallowed be Your name" (v. 2) before it asks for anything. Why might it start there? Christians differ on whether verses 2 to 4 are a set prayer to recite or a pattern for praying in your own words. Which do you find more helpful, and why?

Verse 3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread," and verse 4 links forgiveness to the way "we also forgive everyone who sins against us." Which of these is harder for you right now: trusting God for today, or forgiving someone?

Jesus says, "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you" (v. 9). Has there been something you asked for and did not receive? How do you feel about that, and what do you do with it?
Verse 13 ends with "how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him." What does it tell you that the gift Jesus names is God himself, and not a list of things?

After the healing, the crowds are amazed, some accuse Jesus, and others keep "demanding a sign from heaven" (vv. 14 to 16). Which of these reactions is closest to yours on an ordinary day: amazement, suspicion or wanting more proof?
A woman praises Jesus' mother, and he answers, "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it" (v. 28). What is the difference between admiring Jesus and following him?

Jesus tells the Pharisees, "inside you are full of greed and wickedness" (v. 39), and says they neglect "justice and the love of God" (v. 42). Where do you see a gap between how things look and what is really going on inside, in others or in yourself?
11.life: Each morning this week, take one minute to pray the words of verses 2 to 4 slowly, then add one honest request in your own words. At the end of the week, notice what you asked for and how you felt as you prayed.
11.prayer: Thank God that he is a Father who gives good gifts. Ask him to teach your group to pray, and to show each person what is real on the inside.
11.tip: The woes in verses 42 to 52 can sound harsh next to the gentle Father in verse 13. Help the group see that Jesus speaks them to religious people who should have known better, and invite everyone to ask what they say to us, not just about the Pharisees.

12.open: What is the most unexpected thing you have ever worried about, and did it turn out to matter?
questions: Jesus warns about "the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy" (v. 1). Why does he compare hypocrisy to something that spreads quietly? Where have you seen that happen, in a church, a workplace or a family?

Jesus says, "not one of them is forgotten by God," and that "even the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (vv. 6, 7). What do these small details tell us about how God sees us, and does that feel easy or hard to believe right now?
A man asks Jesus to settle a quarrel over money, and Jesus answers, "Guard yourselves against every form of greed" (v. 15). Why do you think he went past the request to something deeper?
In the story, God says, "You fool! This very night your life will be required of you" (v. 20). What was the farmer's real mistake? Planning ahead seems sensible, so what was wrong with how he did it?

Jesus says, "do not worry about your life" (v. 22), and then adds, "Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?" (v. 25). When worry takes hold of you, what does it feel like, and what has helped, even a little?

Verse 34 says, "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." If someone looked at your calendar and your bank statement, what would they guess you treasure? Be as honest as you are comfortable with.

Jesus says the master who returns will "dress himself to serve" and wait on his servants (v. 37). How does that picture change the way you think about Jesus coming back, especially if you feel unready or unsure about it?
Verse 48 says, "From everyone who has been given much, much will be required." What has been given to you, such as money, time, skills or people, and what might it look like to use it well?
12.life: Pick one thing you tend to worry about and one thing you tend to hold tightly, such as money, time or a plan. This week, bring the worry to God each time it comes up, and do one small, concrete act of generosity with the thing you hold tightly.
12.prayer: Thank God that your Father "is pleased to give you the kingdom" (v. 32). Ask him to loosen your grip on what you cling to, and to quiet the worries each person in the group is carrying.
12.tip: Verses 33 and 34 can make people feel guilty or defensive about money, and Christians differ on whether Jesus means selling possessions literally for everyone or holding wealth loosely and generously. Say that plainly, then steer the group toward verse 34 and the heart question rather than rules about who is giving enough. Also be gentle with verses 4 and 5 and 45 to 48, which sound harsh. You do not need to explain every line; it is fine to say some of it is hard.

13.open: Think of a time you were sure you had missed your chance at something, and then got a second one. What happened?
questions: Some people told Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate, and Jesus asked, "Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans?" (v. 2). When something terrible happens to someone, why do people so often look for a reason they must have deserved it?

Jesus says twice, "unless you repent, you too will all perish" (vv. 3, 5). What do you think he is asking people to do? Christians differ on whether this points mainly to the coming destruction of Jerusalem or to each person's final judgment. How does the warning land with you either way?
In the fig tree story the gardener says, "leave it alone again this year" (v. 8). What does this picture tell you about how God deals with people who are not yet bearing fruit?

The woman had been "hunched over and could not stand up straight" for eighteen years (v. 11). Jesus called her over and set her free, and she "began to glorify God" (v. 13). What stands out to you about how Jesus treats her?
The synagogue leader wanted healing to wait for another day (v. 14). Where can good rules or routines get in the way of caring for someone in front of us?
Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed and to leaven (vv. 19, 21). Where have you seen something small and easy to overlook grow into something that mattered?

Someone asks if only a few will be saved, and Jesus says, "Make every effort to enter through the narrow door" (v. 24). He does not answer with a number. What do you make of that, and what questions does it leave you with? It is fine to say you are unsure.
Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children "as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling" (v. 34). What does this picture tell you about his heart toward people who turn away?
13.life: Pick one person you have been quietly judging, or one hard event you have tried to explain away. This week, set the judging aside and do one small kind thing for that person or for someone hurting.
13.prayer: Thank God for his patience with us, and for Jesus' longing to gather us in. Ask for honesty about where you need to turn back to him, and for compassion toward people who are suffering.
13.tip: Verses 24 to 28 can feel frightening, and someone may worry about their own salvation or a loved one's. Don't argue it out. Point to the whole chapter: the patient gardener, the freed woman, the hen gathering her chicks, and the guests coming from every direction (v. 29). Make room for people to say they are uneasy.

14.open: When you walk into a room full of people, where do you usually sit, and why?
questions: Verse 1 says the guests were "watching Him closely," and when Jesus asks if healing on the Sabbath is lawful, "they remained silent" (v. 4). Why do you think they said nothing, and what does Jesus show them about what the Sabbath is for?

Jesus says, "everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted" (v. 11). Where do you see people chasing the best seat today, at work, at school or online? When is it hardest for you to take the lower place?

In his day a dinner invitation came with the expectation of being invited back. Jesus tells his host to invite people who "cannot repay you" (v. 14). Who in your life could you welcome without expecting anything in return?
The guests in the banquet story make excuses about a field, oxen and a marriage (vv. 18-20). None of these are bad things. What good things can crowd out an invitation from God today?
The servant reports, "there is still room" (v. 22). What does that say about God's welcome? If you have ever felt you did not belong at the table, what comes up for you when you read it?
Jesus says whoever does not "carry his cross" cannot be his disciple (v. 27). What would that have sounded like to the crowds then, and what might it mean for us now?

Verses 26 and 33 are hard. Some read the word "hate" as meaning to love family less by comparison, and Christians differ on how literally to take the call to leave family and possessions. How do these verses land with you?
Jesus talks about someone who should "sit down and count the cost" (v. 28). Is there any part of following Jesus you are still weighing or unsure about? Honest answers are welcome here.
14.life: This week, invite someone to a meal or a coffee who could never repay you, or who rarely gets invited anywhere. Pay attention to how it feels to give without expecting anything back.
14.prayer: Thank God for a welcome that does not depend on our status or our record. Ask for honesty about what we are holding onto, and for the courage to follow Jesus with open eyes.
14.tip: Verses 26 and 33 can leave people anxious or guilty. Say that Jesus is being honest about the cost, not trying to shame anyone, and read them alongside the open invitation of the banquet. Let people say how the verses land, and remind them that faithful Christians understand the demands differently.

15.open: Think of a time you were really glad to be found, whether you were lost, locked out or just missing someone. What happened?
questions: The Pharisees and scribes grumbled, "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them" (v. 2). Why would sharing a meal with someone matter so much in that culture, and what does it say about Jesus?
In the first story the shepherd goes after the one that is lost "until he finds it" (v. 4). What does it tell you about God that he goes looking instead of waiting for the sheep to return?
Jesus says there is "joy in the presence of God's angels over one sinner who repents" (v. 10). Is it easy or hard for you to picture God being joyful about you? Be as honest as you like.

The younger son asks for his share of the estate and ends up wishing he could eat what the pigs ate (v. 16). What do you think drew him away, and what do people our age go looking for when they leave home in one way or another?
Verse 17 says he "came to his senses." What do you think brings a person to that moment, and have you seen it happen in someone you know?
While the son was "still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion" (v. 20). What stands out to you about how the father responds before the son says a word?

The older brother says, "All these years I have served you," and he is angry about the celebration (vv. 28-29). Where do you find yourself in this story: the younger son, the older son, or somewhere in between? What makes you say so?
The story ends without telling us whether the older brother goes in to the feast. Why do you think Jesus left it open, and what would going in look like for someone today?
15.life: This week, think of one person who feels far from God or from your community. Pray for them by name each day, and look for one simple way to welcome them, like an invitation, a message or a shared meal.
15.prayer: Thank God that he goes looking for the lost and that "this son of mine was dead and is alive again" is the kind of welcome he gives. Ask him to help each of you receive that welcome and to share it with others without grudging.
15.tip: People often feel strongly about the older brother, and some will defend him because his anger sounds fair. Let that be said without rushing to correct it. Then point out that the father goes out to him too and pleads with him (v. 28), so the story treats the loyal son with the same tenderness. Also note that Christians differ on whether the main focus is the welcome of the returning sinner or the challenge to the resentful older brother, and the chapter can hold both.

16.open: Tell us about a time you made a plan quickly because you were out of options. How did it turn out?
questions: The manager says, "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg" (v. 3). What does his panic tell you about him, and where have you felt that kind of pressure about money or security?
The master commended the manager "because he had acted shrewdly" (v. 8). Jesus is praising his foresight, not his honesty. What do you make of Jesus using a questionable character as an example?

Jesus says, "use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves" (v. 9). Many readers take this to mean using money to help people in need. What would that look like in your own life, not just in theory?
Verse 13 says, "You cannot serve both God and money." How can you tell which one is actually running your life? What are the quiet signs?
In verse 15 Jesus says, "God knows your hearts." Is that comforting or uncomfortable to you right now? Be as honest as you like, including if the answer is somewhere in the middle.

Lazarus lay "at his gate" and the rich man still lived "each day in joyous splendor" (vv. 20, 19). What do you think makes it possible to pass the same person in need day after day and stop really seeing them?

Christians differ on whether this story describes what really happens after death or is a parable using familiar Jewish pictures of the afterlife to make a point about wealth and neglect. Either way, what do you think Jesus most wants his listeners to take from it?
Abraham says, "They have Moses and the Prophets" (v. 29). The rich man thinks a dramatic sign would change his brothers. Why might a sign not be enough, and what actually changes a heart?
16.life: Look at your spending or your calendar this week and pick one specific way to help someone in need, whether with money, time or a visit. Do it, and notice what it stirs up in you.
16.prayer: Ask God to show you who is at your gate, someone you have stopped seeing. Ask for a generous heart and for honesty about where money has too much hold on you.
16.tip: Verses 1 to 8 confuse almost everyone, and people may get stuck on whether Jesus approves of cheating. Say plainly that scholars disagree about what the manager did, and bring the group back to verse 9 and the point about using money wisely for others. Also, the second story can make people anxious about hell or about wealth. Keep the focus on the rich man's neglect of Lazarus rather than on debating the afterlife.

17.open: Think of a time someone did something kind for you and you never properly thanked them. What do you remember about it?
questions: Jesus says, "Watch yourselves" and then speaks of rebuking and forgiving (v. 3). Why might it be hard to do both, to be honest about a wrong and to forgive?
Verse 4 says forgiveness may be needed "seven times in a day." Where does forgiving feel hardest for you, and what makes it so?
The apostles ask, "Increase our faith!" (v. 5). Jesus answers with a mustard seed (v. 6). What do you think he is telling them about the size and the source of faith?
The servant story ends with, "We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty" (v. 10). Many people hear this as harsh. How do you hear it, and how might it free us from keeping score with God?
The ten lepers cried out, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" (v. 13). Have you ever asked God for help while feeling unsure he would answer? What was that like?
Only one man returned, "praising God in a loud voice" (v. 15), and he was a Samaritan. Why do you think the outsider was the one who came back, and why do the rest of us so easily move on?
Jesus says, "the kingdom of God is in your midst" (v. 21). What would it look like to notice God's kingdom already at work around you, in ordinary places?
Jesus says, "Whoever tries to save his life will lose it" (v. 33), and warns, "Remember Lot's wife!" (v. 32). What are we tempted to hold onto too tightly, and what might it mean to loosen our grip?
17.life: Each day this week, thank one person out loud or in writing, and thank God for one specific thing, just as the Samaritan came back to do.
17.prayer: Thank God for his mercy that meets us where we are. Ask for a heart that notices his gifts and returns to say thanks, and for the grace to forgive someone you are struggling with.
17.tip: Verses 26 to 37 are the hardest part, and Christians differ on whether they point to AD 70, to Jesus' return, or to both. Say so in one line, then steer the group to what is clear: be ready, stay thankful, and hold things loosely. Don't let the group get stuck on who is 'taken' in verses 34 and 35.

18.open: What is the longest you have ever waited for something you really wanted, and how did you handle the wait?
questions: Luke says Jesus told the first parable about the need "to pray at all times and not lose heart" (v. 1). What tends to make you lose heart when you pray, and what do you do when it happens?

Jesus asks, "Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?" (v. 7). The judge is a contrast to God, not a picture of him. What does that tell us about how God hears us, and how do you hold that alongside times when help seems slow?
The second parable is for people who "viewed others with contempt" (v. 9). Where do you catch yourself quietly comparing your life, faith or choices with other people's?

The tax collector prays only, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner!" (v. 13). Why do you think Jesus says this short prayer sent him home right with God? What would it be like to pray that honestly this week?

The disciples tried to stop parents bringing their babies, but Jesus says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (v. 16). What do you think it means to receive God's kingdom like a child, and who might we be tempted to wave away?

Jesus tells the ruler, "You still lack one thing" (v. 22), and the man becomes very sad. Christians differ on whether this call to sell everything is for every follower or was aimed at this one man. Either way, what might Jesus point to in our own lives that we hold on to tightly?

When the crowd asks, "Who then can be saved?" Jesus answers, "What is impossible with man is possible with God" (v. 27). Where do you feel something is out of your hands, and how does this verse land with you today?

The blind man calls out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (v. 38), and Jesus asks him, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (v. 41). If Jesus asked you that tonight, what would you honestly say, even if you are unsure he will answer?
18.life: Pick one thing you have been asking God for and keep bringing it to him every day this week, even briefly. Add the tax collector's words, "God, have mercy on me," as a way to start each time you pray.
18.prayer: Thank God that he listens to people who cry out to him and welcomes them as a loving Father. Ask for a humble heart, honest words, and the patience to keep praying.
18.tip: The rich ruler story can make people defensive or anxious about money. Don't try to settle what Jesus' words mean for every person. Point the group to verse 27 and to Jesus' kindness toward the man, and invite people to share what they hold on to, not what they think others should give up.

19.open: Think of a time someone welcomed you warmly when you did not expect it. What did it feel like?
questions: Zacchaeus was "a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy" (v. 2), and he ran ahead and climbed a tree just to see Jesus (v. 4). What does that tell you about him, and what do you think he was hoping for?
Jesus says, "Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today" (v. 5). He invites himself in, before Zacchaeus has said or done anything. Why do you think Jesus begins that way?
The crowd grumbles, "He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!" (v. 7). When have you been tempted to feel that someone did not deserve kindness? Or when have you been the one on the outside?

Zacchaeus promises to give away half his possessions and repay fourfold anyone he cheated (v. 8). Which came first for him, a changed life or being welcomed? What does that suggest for how change usually happens?

Jesus says, "the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (v. 10). Where do you feel lost, stuck or far from God right now? Say as much or as little as you like, including if you are not sure what you believe.
In the story of the minas, the servant who hid his money says, "I was afraid of you" (v. 21). How might fear keep us from using what we have been given? What helps you move past it?

Some Pharisees tell Jesus to quiet his followers, and he says, "the very stones will cry out" (v. 40). Then he weeps over Jerusalem (v. 41). What do the cheering, the grumbling and the tears show you about Jesus?
The chapter ends with Jesus in the temple saying it should be "a house of prayer" (v. 46). What would help your own life, or your church, feel more like that?
19.life: Zacchaeus was welcomed first, and then he changed. This week, make room for one person who is easy to overlook or avoid: share a meal, send a message or simply listen. Notice what it costs you and what happens.
19.prayer: Thank Jesus that he came "to seek and to save the lost." Ask him to show you where you are hiding or holding back, and to give you his welcome for others.
19.tip: The parable of the minas ends with the king ordering his enemies killed (v. 27), and people will likely be troubled. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether this king stands for Jesus or contrasts with him. Do not try to settle it. Keep the group on the servants and the question of fear and trust, and let people say that it bothers them.

20.open: Think of a time you were put on the spot with a hard question. How did you handle it?
questions: The leaders ask, "by what authority are You doing these things" (v. 2). When Jesus turns the question back, they say "they did not know where it was from" (v. 7) because an honest answer would cost them. When are you tempted to give a safe answer instead of a true one?
In the parable the owner says, "I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him." (v. 13) What does this say about the owner's patience, and what do you make of that as a picture of God?

Jesus quotes, "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (v. 17). Christians read this as Jesus, rejected and then raised up. Why might people reject someone who threatens their position? Where do we push back when Jesus asks something of us?

Christians differ on whether the vineyard being given to others means God replaced Israel with the church, or means leadership was taken from those particular leaders while God's commitment to the Jewish people remains. However you read it, how can we hear this parable without turning it against anyone today?

Jesus says, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s." (v. 25) What do you think belongs to each? Some readers take "what is God's" to mean people themselves, who bear God's image. How does that change your answer?

Jesus says, "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive." (v. 38) What hopes, doubts or questions come up for you when you think about life after death? Be as honest as you like.
Jesus asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord (vv. 41-44). Who do you say Jesus is right now, and what questions do you still have about him?
Jesus warns about teachers who love honor and "for a show make lengthy prayers" (v. 47). Where are we tempted to make faith a performance, and what does it look like to be real instead?
20.life: This week, do one quiet kindness for someone with little power or voice, such as an elderly neighbor, a widow or a single parent, and tell no one about it.
20.prayer: Ask God to give you honesty when a question is uncomfortable. Pray for a faith that is real and not for show, and for trust in the God of the living.
20.tip: The parable is violent and verse 18 sounds harsh, so some may feel uneasy. Say that Jesus was speaking to leaders who were about to reject him, not to a whole people. Keep the focus on our own hearts, and do not let the discussion drift into blaming any group today.

21.open: What is something you own or a place you love that you hope never changes?
questions: Jesus says the widow "out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on" (v. 4). What do you think he saw in her gift that others missed?
Some readers hear praise for the widow here, and others hear sorrow over a system that took from the poor. Which do you hear, and why?
The disciples admired the temple's "beautiful stones" (v. 5), and Jesus said "not one stone will be left on another" (v. 6). What do people today treat as solid and permanent that might not be?
Jesus warns, "See to it that you are not deceived" (v. 8). How do you tell the difference between a voice worth trusting and one that plays on fear?
Jesus tells his followers, "make up your mind not to worry beforehand how to defend yourselves" (v. 14). When have you felt unprepared to speak up for what you believe, and what happened?

In verse 16 he says some will be betrayed, and some put to death, and then adds "not even a hair of your head will perish" (v. 18). How do you make sense of those words standing side by side? It's fine to say you're not sure.
Verse 28 says, "stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near." What would it look like to face hard news with your head up rather than bowed in fear?
Verse 34 warns that "the worries of life" can weigh down our hearts. What tends to weigh yours down lately, and what helps you keep watch and pray (v. 36)?
21.life: Each day this week, set aside five minutes to put your phone down and pray about the news or worry that is weighing on you most. Then do one small, quiet act of generosity, even if it is only a few coins' worth.
21.prayer: Ask God for strength to stay steady when things that seemed solid shake. Pray for anyone in the group carrying heavy worries, and for a heart that gives and trusts like the widow's.
21.tip: Verses 25 to 36 are a magnet for end-times speculation, and Christians differ on whether they describe AD 70, Jesus' return, or both. Say that plainly in one sentence, then steer back to what Jesus asks of us: do not be deceived, do not be anxious, keep watch and pray. If someone brings a timeline, thank them and move on.

22.open: When did you last share a meal that you still remember, and what made it stand out?
questions: Jesus says, "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering" (v. 15). What does it tell you that he wanted this meal with his friends, knowing what was coming?

At the table Jesus says of the bread, "This is My body, given for you," and of the cup, "the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you" (vv. 19, 20). What do you think he wanted the disciples to understand about his death?

Christians differ on what the bread and cup are: some believe they truly become his body and blood, some believe he is present in them in a real way, and some see them as a symbol of remembrance. How have you experienced communion, and what has it meant to you?

Right after the meal the disciples argue about "which of them should be considered the greatest" (v. 24). Jesus says, "the one who leads like the one who serves" (v. 26). Where do you see the pull to be noticed or important, and what would serving look like there?

In the garden Jesus prays, "Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done" (v. 42). What do you make of Jesus asking to be spared? Is there a prayer you have found hard to pray like this?

Peter said, "I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death" (v. 33), and hours later he said, "I do not know Him" (v. 57). What do you think we can really know about how we will act under pressure?

Luke says "the Lord turned and looked at Peter," and Peter "went outside and wept bitterly" (vv. 61, 62). What do you imagine was in that look? Where do you need to hear that failure is not the end of the story, or find it hard to believe that?

When Jesus is arrested, one disciple strikes with a sword, and Jesus says, "No more of this!" and heals the man's ear (v. 51). What does this show about the kind of kingdom Jesus brings and how he treats those who oppose him?
22.life: Jesus told his friends, "Pray that you will not enter into temptation" (v. 40). This week, name one area where you feel sure you are strong, and ask God each morning to keep you faithful there. If you have failed someone recently, take one step to make it right.
22.prayer: Thank Jesus that he gave his body and poured out his blood for us. Ask for humility to serve instead of seeking to be greatest, and for faithfulness when we are under pressure. Pray for anyone in the group who feels they have let God down.
22.tip: The question about communion can pull the group into a debate. Say plainly that Christians differ, invite people to share what it has meant to them rather than to argue a position, and keep the focus on Jesus's love in verses 15 to 20. Peter's failure may also touch people who carry shame, so leave quiet space and don't rush to fix it.

23.open: Think of a time someone gave you a second chance you didn't expect. What happened?
questions: Pilate says, "I find no basis for a charge against this man" (v. 4), and later asks, "What evil has this man done?" (v. 22). Why do you think Luke wants us to hear Jesus declared innocent so many times?
Verse 23 says "their clamor prevailed," and Pilate gave in. When have you felt pressure to go along with something you knew was wrong? What made it hard to hold your ground?
Herod hoped to see a miracle, and Jesus gave him no answer (vv. 8, 9). Why might Jesus stay silent? What do you do when God seems silent to you?
From the cross Jesus says, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (v. 34). What stands out to you about who he prays for and when he prays it?
The rulers say, "He saved others; let Him save Himself" (v. 35). In a way they are right, because he did not save himself. What do you make of that?

One criminal says, "Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!" (v. 42), and Jesus answers, "today you will be with Me in Paradise" (v. 43). He offers no list of good deeds, only a request. What do you notice about that, and what questions or doubts does it raise for you?

Christians understand Jesus' death in different ways. Some stress him taking the punishment others deserved, and others stress an innocent man's faithful death and God's victory over evil. Which parts of this chapter help you think about what the cross means, and where are you still unsure?
23.life: Think of one person who has hurt or wronged you. Each day this week, pray Jesus' words from verse 34 for them by name. You don't have to feel it yet. Just say it and see what happens in you.
23.prayer: Thank Jesus that he stayed faithful all the way to the cross, and that he welcomed a man who simply asked to be remembered. Ask for honesty about where we give in to pressure, and for the courage to forgive.
23.tip: Chapters like this have been misused to blame Jewish people for Jesus' death. Gently keep the focus on the whole cast: the council, Pilate, Herod, the soldiers and the crowd, with Jesus himself a Jew. Invite people to see how easily any of us could be in that crowd.

24.open: Have you ever been so sure about something that you were slow to believe you were wrong? What happened?
questions: The two messengers ask the women, "Why do you look for the living among the dead?" (v. 5). What do you think the women expected to find that morning, and why?
When the women reported what they saw, the others thought it was "nonsense" (v. 11). Why might the people closest to Jesus have found this news so hard to believe?
The two on the road say, "we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel" (v. 21). Have you ever said "we were hoping" about something in your own life? What was that like?
Verse 16 says "their eyes were kept from recognizing Him," even as he walked beside them. When have you realized only later that God was close during a hard stretch?

Jesus "explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself" (v. 27), and afterwards they said their "hearts" were "burning within" them (v. 32). What helps the Bible come alive for you, and what makes it feel flat or confusing?

They recognized Jesus "in the breaking of the bread" (v. 35). Where do you notice Jesus most clearly: in a meal, in a friend, in worship, in quiet, or somewhere else? If you are not sure you notice him anywhere right now, say so honestly.
Jesus meets frightened, doubting people with "Peace be with you" (v. 36) and invites them to "Touch Me and see" (v. 39). What does that tell you about how he treats honest doubt?

Jesus says "repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations" (v. 47) and calls them "witnesses" (v. 48). What might being a witness look like for ordinary people in our everyday lives?
24.life: This week, tell one person about a time you felt hope return after you thought it was gone. Keep it short and honest. If that feels like too much, write it down and thank God for it.
24.prayer: Thank Jesus for meeting doubting and discouraged people where they are. Ask him to open our eyes to see him this week, and to give us joy like the disciples had at the end of the chapter.
24.tip: Some people will wrestle with whether the resurrection was a literal bodily event, and Christians read the appearances differently. Say that plainly, then point the group to what Luke stresses in verses 39 to 43, and keep room for honest questions without pushing anyone to settle them tonight.
